accordions.heading: What are hepatitis B and C?
accordions.content:
Hepatitis B and hepatitis C are viruses that affect the liver. Hepatitis B can be passed on through sex without a condom, and both can be passed on through blood, for example by sharing needles. They can cause symptoms such as tiredness, a high temperature or yellowing of the skin and eyes, but many people have no noticeable symptoms at all.

Many adults recover from a new hepatitis B infection on their own within a few months. Some develop a long-term infection that needs monitoring or treatment. Hepatitis C can usually be cured with antiviral tablets.

accordions.heading: Is this for you?
accordions.content:
You don’t need to have symptoms to test. Hepatitis B and C can cause no noticeable symptoms.

It may be worth testing if:
checklist: You have a new sexual partner, or more than one
A sexual partner has told you they have hepatitis B, hepatitis C or another STI
You’ve shared needles or other equipment for injecting drugs

benefits.heading: Test privately
benefits.text: Everything you need to test for hepatitis B and C at home:

how.heading: How does the test work?
how.intro:
The test checks a small finger-prick blood sample for two markers. For hepatitis B, it looks for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), which may indicate a current infection. For hepatitis C, it looks for antibodies your body makes in response to the virus, which can remain after an infection has cleared or been cured.

Your result appears on the test pad in around 15 minutes, with no sample to send to a laboratory.

steps.title: Prick your finger
steps.text: Wash your hands and clean your fingertip with an alcohol pad. Let it dry, then use the lancet to prick your finger and form a drop of blood.

steps.title: Add blood and diluent
steps.text: Use the pipette to collect your blood. Add 3 drops of blood to each sample well on the test pad, followed by 2 drops of diluent to each well.

steps.title: Read your results
steps.text: Read both results between 15 and 20 minutes. Don't read the test after 30 minutes, as the results may no longer be reliable.

windows.heading: When should I test?
windows.subheading: You can test now, but an early negative may need repeating. For hepatitis B, this may be at 12 weeks after exposure.

groups.intro:
Read your test between 15 and 20 minutes. Don’t read it after 30 minutes.

Your test pad has two windows: HBsAg for hepatitis B and HCV for hepatitis C. Read each one separately. C is the control line. T is the test line. If both windows show lines at C and T, both results are positive.

items.title: Negative for both
items.text: One line at C only, in both windows. No hepatitis B surface antigen or hepatitis C antibodies were detected.

items.title: Hepatitis B positive
items.text: Lines at C and T in the hepatitis B window, even if the T line is faint. Hepatitis B surface antigen was detected.

items.title: Hepatitis C positive
items.text: Lines at C and T in the hepatitis C window, even if the T line is faint. Hepatitis C antibodies were detected.

items.title: Invalid
items.text: No line at C in one or both windows, even if a T line appears. The test has not worked. Contact us and we’ll help.

notes.title: Good to know
notes.text: This test is designed for screening and doesn’t replace advice from a doctor or nurse. For ages 16 and over.

questions.question: How soon after a possible exposure can I test?
questions.answer:
You can test now, but an early negative may need repeating. For hepatitis B, this may be at 12 weeks after exposure.

Hepatitis C: an early negative result may need repeating at six months.

If you have symptoms, know you have been exposed or want advice about testing sooner, contact your GP or a sexual health clinic.

questions.question: How reliable is this hepatitis B and C rapid test?
questions.answer:
When used correctly, this test provides a reliable way to check for hepatitis B and hepatitis C at home.

Testing too soon after exposure can affect your result, so an early negative may need to be repeated. This is a screening test, so a positive result should be followed up with a sexual health clinic or your GP for further testing.

questions.question: What does a negative result mean?
questions.answer:
A negative result means hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibodies were not detected by the test.

If your possible exposure was recent, you may have tested too early. If you have symptoms or are still concerned, speak to a sexual health clinic or your GP.

questions.question: What if my result is positive?
questions.answer:
If your test is positive for hepatitis B, hepatitis C or both, you'll need further testing to confirm what the result means. A positive hepatitis B result may indicate a current infection, while a positive hepatitis C result could mean you have the infection now or had it in the past.

Contact a sexual health clinic or your GP as soon as possible. They'll explain your result and whether you need treatment. Hepatitis C can usually be cured with tablets, and many adults recover naturally from a new hepatitis B infection.

NHS sexual health services are free and confidential.

questions.question: Can I use this test if I’ve been vaccinated against hepatitis B?
questions.answer:
Yes. The hepatitis B vaccine doesn't normally cause a positive result on this test because it looks for hepatitis B surface antigen, not the protective antibodies produced after vaccination.

This test cannot tell you whether you're immune to hepatitis B.

questions.question: I’ve had hepatitis C before. Can I use this test?
questions.answer:
Hepatitis C antibodies can stay in your blood after the infection has cleared or been treated, so the hepatitis C line may still show a positive result.

A sexual health clinic or your GP can arrange an HCV RNA blood test to check whether the virus is currently present.

questions.question: Can I take a hepatitis B and C test while pregnant?
questions.answer: If you’re pregnant and concerned about hepatitis B or C, speak to your midwife, GP or a sexual health clinic. Hepatitis B testing is routinely offered during pregnancy through the NHS.
